Emerging Hot Spot Analysis

Author

Davin Cuaso

Published

3 October 2026

Modified

3 October 2026

Overview

This exercise works through Chapter 11: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis, using the supplied Hunan county and GDP-per-capita files. Code is adapted for the installed package versions, with extra checks and explanations. Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) looks beyond a single map. It identifies where local hot spots and cold spots occur in each year, tests whether those local patterns are changing, and gives each county a final pattern label.

The workflow has four parts:

  1. organise the county records as a space-time cube;
  2. calculate local Getis-Ord Gi* for every county and year;
  3. test each county’s Gi* series for a monotonic trend with the Mann-Kendall test; and
  4. classify the history of each county as a hot spot, cold spot, or no detected pattern.

Data and preparation

The two datasets are the files distributed with the course exercise.

Dataset Source Use
Hunan county boundary Official In-Class Exercise 6 files County geometry and spatial relationships
Hunan_GDPPC.csv Official In-Class Exercise 6 file Annual county GDP per capita from 2005 to 2021

st_read() imports the polygons and st_transform() places them in EPSG 32650, a projected coordinate system measured in metres. read.csv() imports the time-series table.

Show the R code 
hunan <- st_read(
  dsn = file.path(data_path, "geospatial"),
  layer = "Hunan",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32650)

GDPPC <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "Hunan_GDPPC.csv"))
# Sort keys before constructing the cube and its aligned neighbour columns.
GDPPC <- arrange(GDPPC, Year, County)
hunan <- arrange(hunan, County)

Before continuing, I check that every county has one record in every year and that the names in the attribute table match the names in the boundary file.

Show the R code 
data_checks <- tibble(
  Check = c(
    "County polygons",
    "Counties in the time series",
    "Years",
    "County-year records",
    "Unmatched county names",
    "Missing GDPPC values"
  ),
  Result = c(
    nrow(hunan),
    n_distinct(GDPPC$County),
    n_distinct(GDPPC$Year),
    nrow(GDPPC),
    sum(!unique(GDPPC$County) %in% hunan$County),
    sum(is.na(GDPPC$GDPPC))
  )
)

knitr::kable(data_checks, caption = "Checks on the two input datasets")
Checks on the two input datasets
Check Result
County polygons 88
Counties in the time series 88
Years 17
County-year records 1496
Unmatched county names 0
Missing GDPPC values 0
Show the R code 
stopifnot(
  nrow(hunan) == 88,
  n_distinct(GDPPC$County) == 88,
  n_distinct(GDPPC$Year) == 17,
  nrow(GDPPC) == 88 * 17,
  all(unique(GDPPC$County) %in% hunan$County),
  !anyNA(GDPPC$GDPPC),
  !anyDuplicated(GDPPC[c("County", "Year")]),
  setequal(GDPPC$County, hunan$County),
  all(is.finite(GDPPC$GDPPC)),
  all(st_is_valid(hunan))
)

The checks confirm a balanced dataset: 88 counties observed in each of 17 years, for 1,496 county-year records.

Creating the space-time cube

spacetime() links the yearly GDPPC records to the matching county geometry. The county field is the location key and Year is the time key.

Show the R code 
GDPPC_st <- spacetime(
  GDPPC,
  hunan,
  .loc_col = "County",
  .time_col = "Year"
)

cube_check <- tibble(
  Test = "Is GDPPC_st a valid space-time cube?",
  Result = is_spacetime_cube(GDPPC_st)
)

knitr::kable(cube_check, caption = "Space-time cube validation")
Space-time cube validation
Test Result
Is GDPPC_st a valid space-time cube? TRUE

The TRUE result means that the location and time identifiers form a regular cube. This matters because the EHSA functions expect every time slice to use the same locations in the same order.

Computing local Gi*

Deriving spatial weights

The chapter workflow first activates the cube’s geometry context. st_contiguity() finds counties that touch, while include_self() includes the county itself as required by Gi*. st_inverse_distance() gives closer neighbours more influence. set_nbs() and set_wts() then copy the same spatial structure to every annual slice.

Show the R code 
GDPPC_nb <- GDPPC_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(
    nb = include_self(st_contiguity(geometry)),
    wt = st_inverse_distance(
      nb,
      geometry,
      scale = 1,
      alpha = 1
    ),
    .before = 1
  ) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")

weight_check <- GDPPC_nb %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(
    `Minimum links, including self` = min(lengths(nb)),
    `Average links, including self` = round(mean(lengths(nb)), 2),
    `Maximum links, including self` = max(lengths(nb))
  )

knitr::kable(weight_check, caption = "Neighbour-list check")
Neighbour-list check
Minimum links, including self Average links, including self Maximum links, including self
2 6.09 12

In sfdep 0.2.5, a zero-distance inverse weight is set to zero. The self-link is therefore present but contributes no GDPPC to this intermediate weighted sum. I retain that setting to reproduce the chapter, but it differs from the usual positive-self-weight Gi*. The final EHSA call below uses its own contiguity weights with a positive self-weight.

The order of the records must not be changed after set_nbs() and set_wts(). These list-columns are aligned to the rows of each time slice.

Calculating Gi* for each year

For each year, local_gstar_perm() compares a county and its neighbours with the province-wide pattern. A positive Gi* value points towards a local concentration of high GDPPC values. A negative value points towards a concentration of low values. The permutation procedure evaluates how unusual the observed local statistic is under spatial randomness.

Show the R code 
set.seed(6262026)

# Preserve the nb object's class: newer dplyr versions strip it in grouped list-columns.
geo_context <- GDPPC_nb |> activate("geometry")
annual_nb <- geo_context$nb
annual_wt <- geo_context$wt
stopifnot(inherits(annual_nb, "nb"))
gi_stars <- as.data.frame(GDPPC) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  group_modify(~bind_cols(.x, local_gstar_perm(
    .x$GDPPC, annual_nb, annual_wt, nsim = 999, iseed = 6262026
  ))) |>
  ungroup()

gi_preview <- gi_stars %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Year, County, GDPPC, gi_star, p_value, p_folded_sim) %>%
  slice_head(n = 8)

knitr::kable(
  gi_preview,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "First eight county-year Gi* results"
)
First eight county-year Gi* results
Year County GDPPC gi_star p_value p_folded_sim
2005 Anhua 4411 -0.7919 0.4186 0.203
2005 Anren 7423 1.5666 0.1345 0.082
2005 Anxiang 8184 0.3771 0.7371 0.309

The Gi* statistic describes the local spatial context of GDPPC. It is not a direct measure of how quickly a county’s own GDPPC grew.

Mann-Kendall trend test

The Mann-Kendall test asks whether a sequence tends to move consistently upward or downward through time.

  • Null hypothesis: there is no monotonic trend in the county’s Gi* series.
  • Alternative hypothesis: a monotonic trend is present.
  • Tau: values near 1 indicate an upward trend, while values near -1 indicate a downward trend.
  • p-value: a value below 0.05 provides evidence against the null hypothesis.

Changsha example

The chapter uses Changsha to demonstrate the calculation.

Show the R code 
cbg <- gi_stars %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(County == "Changsha") %>%
  select(County, Year, gi_star)
Show the R code 
p <- ggplot(cbg, aes(x = Year, y = gi_star)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(min(cbg$Year), max(cbg$Year), by = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gi* statistic") +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

p

The same chart can be explored interactively by hovering over each year.

Show the R code 
ggplotly(p)
Show the R code 
changsha_mk <- cbg %>%
  summarise(
    mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest_wider(mk)

knitr::kable(
  changsha_mk,
  digits = 5,
  caption = "Mann-Kendall test for Changsha's Gi* series"
)
Mann-Kendall test for Changsha’s Gi* series
tau sl S D varS
0.73529 0.00005 100 136 589.3333

For Changsha, tau is 0.735 and the p-value, reported as sl, is 0.0000454. The positive tau indicates an upward trend in the local Gi* series. At the 5% level, the result is statistically significant. Tau describes the direction of ordering; it is not an annual growth rate.

Testing all counties

The same test is repeated for each county. Sorting by the p-value brings the strongest evidence of monotonic change to the top.

Show the R code 
county_mk <- gi_stars %>%
  group_by(County) %>%
  summarise(
    mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star))),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest_wider(mk)

emerging <- county_mk %>%
  arrange(sl, desc(abs(tau))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  transmute(
    County,
    Tau = tau,
    `p-value` = sl,
    Direction = if_else(tau > 0, "Upward Gi* trend", "Downward Gi* trend")
  )

knitr::kable(
  emerging,
  digits = 6,
  caption = "Ten strongest monotonic Gi* trends"
)

Zhuzhou 0.867647 0.000001 Upward Gi* trend
Xinning -0.852941 0.000002 Downward Gi* trend

The three smallest p-values belong to Shaoshan, Shuangfeng, Zhuzhou. This table identifies a change in local spatial association, not yet a complete EHSA class. The final classification also considers which individual years were significant hot spots or cold spots.

Performing Emerging Hot Spot Analysis

emerging_hotspot_analysis() combines the annual Gi* histories with the Mann-Kendall trend. Following the chapter, one time lag and 99 simulations are used. The package’s classification threshold is explicitly set to 0.01, its current default. This final call builds its own row-standardised contiguity weights; it does not inherit the inverse-distance weights used above. Its output p_value is the Mann–Kendall trend p-value. The internal bin test uses a folded simulation tail; it should not be described as a two-sided 5% test or as FDR-adjusted. The chapter introduces FDR conceptually, but this call does not apply it.

Show the R code 
set.seed(6262026)

ehsa <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(
  x = GDPPC_st,
  .var = "GDPPC",
  k = 1,
  nsim = 99,
  threshold = 0.01,
  include_gi = TRUE
)

ehsa_display <- ehsa %>%
  mutate(
    classification = classification %>%
      str_replace("^oscilating", "oscillating") %>%
      str_to_sentence()
  )

Distribution of EHSA classes

Show the R code 
class_counts <- ehsa_display %>%
  count(classification, sort = TRUE)

ggplot(
  class_counts,
  aes(x = reorder(classification, n), y = n)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3182bd", width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.8) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.10))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of counties") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())

The largest class is Sporadic coldspot, with 46 counties. These labels depend on the simulation seed, threshold and package implementation. The count chart includes all counties; the map below applies an additional trend filter.

Mapping significant EHSA results

The EHSA table is joined to the county polygons by the named county field. In keeping with the chapter, only counties with Mann-Kendall p-values below 0.05 are coloured. The legend is placed outside the map so it does not cover any county.

Show the R code 
hunan_ehsa <- hunan %>%
  left_join(
    ehsa_display,
    by = join_by(County == location)
  )

ehsa_sig <- hunan_ehsa %>%
  filter(p_value < 0.05)

stopifnot(
  nrow(hunan_ehsa) == nrow(hunan),
  nrow(ehsa_sig) == sum(ehsa_display$p_value < 0.05)
)
Show the R code 
ehsa_colours <- c(
  "Consecutive hotspot" = "#b2182b",
  "Sporadic hotspot" = "#ef8a62",
  "Oscillating hotspot" = "#fddbc7",
  "Sporadic coldspot" = "#67a9cf",
  "Oscillating coldspot" = "#2166ac",
  "No pattern detected" = "#bdbdbd"
)

# ggplot2 provides the same categorical map without tmap version dependencies.
# Neutral background counties remain visible; only trend-significant classes are coloured.
ggplot(hunan_ehsa) +
  geom_sf(fill = "#f0f2f4", colour = "#9e9e9e", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = ehsa_sig, aes(fill = classification), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ehsa_colours, name = "EHSA class") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Emerging GDPPC hot and cold spot patterns",
       caption = "Only counties with Mann–Kendall p < 0.05 are coloured; grey is not evidence of no clustering.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())

There are 44 counties with a Mann-Kendall p-value below 0.05. The coloured counties pass the trend filter. A county can still have significant hot years yet remain grey if its overall trend is not significant. This distinction matters especially for persistent patterns, which need not have a trend.

Reading the class labels

The labels summarise both the timing of significant Gi* results and the trend in their intensity.

  • New: significant only in the final period, with no earlier significant result of the same type.
  • Consecutive: an uninterrupted run at the end of the series, covering fewer than 90% of all periods.
  • Intensifying or diminishing: significant in at least 90% of periods, including the last period, with a significant upward or downward intensity trend.
  • Persistent: significant in at least 90% of periods without a clear upward or downward intensity trend.
  • Sporadic: significant in some, but fewer than 90%, of the periods and never significant as the opposite type.
  • Oscillating: significant in the final period but was also significant as the opposite type in an earlier period.
  • Historical: significant in at least 90% of periods, but not significant in the final period.
  • No pattern detected: none of the defined histories applies.

The hot spot and cold spot versions use the same timing rules. Their difference is the sign of the underlying local Gi* pattern.

Assumptions and limitations

  • County boundaries and neighbour relationships are treated as constant from 2005 to 2021.
  • Inverse-distance weights assume that nearby contiguous counties exert more spatial influence than farther contiguous counties.
  • The Mann-Kendall test detects a monotonic direction. It does not require a straight-line trend, but its usual p-value assumes independent observations. Serial dependence can make apparent trends look more convincing than they are.
  • GDPPC is analysed as supplied. Without a price adjustment, changes in the raw values may include inflation. The Gi* trend should therefore be read as a change in relative local clustering, not as a pure measure of real economic growth.
  • With 99 simulations, the permutation p-values have fairly coarse resolution. More simulations would provide more stable tail probabilities at the cost of longer computation.
  • Statistical significance does not explain why a county became a hot spot or cold spot. Policy, industry, population, and measurement changes would need separate investigation.

Multiple-testing check

Testing 88 counties creates more opportunities for false positives. Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment is added here for the annual-Gi* trend tests. This is a separate check; it does not silently change the chapter’s EHSA labels or correct the internal bin tests.

Show the R code 
county_mk <- county_mk |> mutate(q_value = p.adjust(sl, method = "BH"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Rule = c("Unadjusted p < 0.05", "BH-adjusted q < 0.05"),
  Counties = c(sum(county_mk$sl < .05), sum(county_mk$q_value < .05))
))
Rule Counties
Unadjusted p < 0.05 46
BH-adjusted q < 0.05 39

What this exercise shows

The checks establish 1496 observations covering 88 counties and 17 years. Changsha’s annual Gi* trend has tau 0.735 and p = 0.0000454. Across all counties, 46 annual-Gi* trend tests pass the unadjusted 5% threshold and 39 pass BH adjustment.

An increasing Gi* series means the county’s local spatial context is becoming more concentrated toward high values relative to the reference distribution. It does not establish a causal explanation or measure GDP growth. The final EHSA adds a temporal neighbourhood and classifies the history; that is a different calculation from testing independently computed annual maps.

References and adaptation notes

  • Kam, Chapter 11: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis: exercise sequence and Hunan example.
  • sfdep source and documentation: cube construction, local statistics and EHSA implementation.
  • spdep Gi and Gi* documentation: permutation statistics and self-neighbours.
  • Mann–Kendall test, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory: interpretation and assumptions.

The interactive chart uses plotly. The categorical map uses ggplot2 rather than tmap; this changes the drawing code, not the EHSA results. The annual permutation count is increased to 999 for a more stable demonstration, while the final EHSA retains the chapter’s 99 simulations so that its computational choices remain visible.

## Overview

This exercise works through [Chapter 11: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap11), using the supplied Hunan county and GDP-per-capita files. Code is adapted for the installed package versions, with extra checks and explanations. Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) looks beyond a single map. It identifies where local hot spots and cold spots occur in each year, tests whether those local patterns are changing, and gives each county a final pattern label.

The workflow has four parts:

1. organise the county records as a space-time cube;
2. calculate local Getis-Ord Gi* for every county and year;
3. test each county's Gi* series for a monotonic trend with the Mann-Kendall test; and
4. classify the history of each county as a hot spot, cold spot, or no detected pattern.

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(sf)
library(sfdep)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(plotly)
library(Kendall)
library(stringr)

options(scipen = 999)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
set.seed(6262026)
data_path <- "data"
```

## Data and preparation

The two datasets are the files distributed with the course exercise.

| Dataset | Source | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Hunan county boundary | [Official In-Class Exercise 6 files](https://github.com/tskam/ISSS626-AY2026-27Aug/tree/master/In-class_Ex/In-class_Ex05/data/geospatial) | County geometry and spatial relationships |
| Hunan_GDPPC.csv | [Official In-Class Exercise 6 file](https://github.com/tskam/ISSS626-AY2026-27Aug/blob/master/In-class_Ex/In-class_Ex05/data/aspatial/Hunan_GDPPC.csv) | Annual county GDP per capita from 2005 to 2021 |

`st_read()` imports the polygons and `st_transform()` places them in EPSG 32650, a projected coordinate system measured in metres. `read.csv()` imports the time-series table.

```{r}
#| label: import-data

hunan <- st_read(
  dsn = file.path(data_path, "geospatial"),
  layer = "Hunan",
  quiet = TRUE
) %>%
  st_transform(crs = 32650)

GDPPC <- read.csv(file.path(data_path, "aspatial", "Hunan_GDPPC.csv"))
# Sort keys before constructing the cube and its aligned neighbour columns.
GDPPC <- arrange(GDPPC, Year, County)
hunan <- arrange(hunan, County)
```

Before continuing, I check that every county has one record in every year and that the names in the attribute table match the names in the boundary file.

```{r}
#| label: data-checks

data_checks <- tibble(
  Check = c(
    "County polygons",
    "Counties in the time series",
    "Years",
    "County-year records",
    "Unmatched county names",
    "Missing GDPPC values"
  ),
  Result = c(
    nrow(hunan),
    n_distinct(GDPPC$County),
    n_distinct(GDPPC$Year),
    nrow(GDPPC),
    sum(!unique(GDPPC$County) %in% hunan$County),
    sum(is.na(GDPPC$GDPPC))
  )
)

knitr::kable(data_checks, caption = "Checks on the two input datasets")

stopifnot(
  nrow(hunan) == 88,
  n_distinct(GDPPC$County) == 88,
  n_distinct(GDPPC$Year) == 17,
  nrow(GDPPC) == 88 * 17,
  all(unique(GDPPC$County) %in% hunan$County),
  !anyNA(GDPPC$GDPPC),
  !anyDuplicated(GDPPC[c("County", "Year")]),
  setequal(GDPPC$County, hunan$County),
  all(is.finite(GDPPC$GDPPC)),
  all(st_is_valid(hunan))
)
```

The checks confirm a balanced dataset: 88 counties observed in each of 17 years, for 1,496 county-year records.

## Creating the space-time cube

`spacetime()` links the yearly GDPPC records to the matching county geometry. The county field is the location key and Year is the time key.

```{r}
#| label: create-cube

GDPPC_st <- spacetime(
  GDPPC,
  hunan,
  .loc_col = "County",
  .time_col = "Year"
)

cube_check <- tibble(
  Test = "Is GDPPC_st a valid space-time cube?",
  Result = is_spacetime_cube(GDPPC_st)
)

knitr::kable(cube_check, caption = "Space-time cube validation")
```

The `TRUE` result means that the location and time identifiers form a regular cube. This matters because the EHSA functions expect every time slice to use the same locations in the same order.

## Computing local Gi*

### Deriving spatial weights

The chapter workflow first activates the cube's geometry context. `st_contiguity()` finds counties that touch, while `include_self()` includes the county itself as required by Gi*. `st_inverse_distance()` gives closer neighbours more influence. `set_nbs()` and `set_wts()` then copy the same spatial structure to every annual slice.

```{r}
#| label: spatial-weights

GDPPC_nb <- GDPPC_st %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  mutate(
    nb = include_self(st_contiguity(geometry)),
    wt = st_inverse_distance(
      nb,
      geometry,
      scale = 1,
      alpha = 1
    ),
    .before = 1
  ) %>%
  set_nbs("nb") %>%
  set_wts("wt")

weight_check <- GDPPC_nb %>%
  activate("geometry") %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  summarise(
    `Minimum links, including self` = min(lengths(nb)),
    `Average links, including self` = round(mean(lengths(nb)), 2),
    `Maximum links, including self` = max(lengths(nb))
  )

knitr::kable(weight_check, caption = "Neighbour-list check")
```

In sfdep 0.2.5, a zero-distance inverse weight is set to zero. The self-link is therefore present but contributes no GDPPC to this intermediate weighted sum. I retain that setting to reproduce the chapter, but it differs from the usual positive-self-weight Gi*. The final EHSA call below uses its own contiguity weights with a positive self-weight.

The order of the records must not be changed after `set_nbs()` and `set_wts()`. These list-columns are aligned to the rows of each time slice.

### Calculating Gi* for each year

For each year, `local_gstar_perm()` compares a county and its neighbours with the province-wide pattern. A positive Gi* value points towards a local concentration of high GDPPC values. A negative value points towards a concentration of low values. The permutation procedure evaluates how unusual the observed local statistic is under spatial randomness.

```{r}
#| label: local-gstar

set.seed(6262026)

# Preserve the nb object's class: newer dplyr versions strip it in grouped list-columns.
geo_context <- GDPPC_nb |> activate("geometry")
annual_nb <- geo_context$nb
annual_wt <- geo_context$wt
stopifnot(inherits(annual_nb, "nb"))
gi_stars <- as.data.frame(GDPPC) |>
  group_by(Year) |>
  group_modify(~bind_cols(.x, local_gstar_perm(
    .x$GDPPC, annual_nb, annual_wt, nsim = 999, iseed = 6262026
  ))) |>
  ungroup()

gi_preview <- gi_stars %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  select(Year, County, GDPPC, gi_star, p_value, p_folded_sim) %>%
  slice_head(n = 8)

knitr::kable(
  gi_preview,
  digits = 4,
  caption = "First eight county-year Gi* results"
)
```

The Gi* statistic describes the local spatial context of GDPPC. It is not a direct measure of how quickly a county's own GDPPC grew.

## Mann-Kendall trend test

The Mann-Kendall test asks whether a sequence tends to move consistently upward or downward through time.

- **Null hypothesis:** there is no monotonic trend in the county's Gi* series.
- **Alternative hypothesis:** a monotonic trend is present.
- **Tau:** values near 1 indicate an upward trend, while values near -1 indicate a downward trend.
- **p-value:** a value below 0.05 provides evidence against the null hypothesis.

### Changsha example

The chapter uses Changsha to demonstrate the calculation.

```{r}
#| label: changsha-series

cbg <- gi_stars %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(County == "Changsha") %>%
  select(County, Year, gi_star)
```

```{r}
#| label: changsha-plot
#| fig-cap: "Local Gi* series for Changsha"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5

p <- ggplot(cbg, aes(x = Year, y = gi_star)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_line(colour = "#2c7fb8", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(min(cbg$Year), max(cbg$Year), by = 2)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Gi* statistic") +
  theme_light(base_size = 12)

p
```

The same chart can be explored interactively by hovering over each year.

```{r}
#| label: changsha-interactive

ggplotly(p)
```

```{r}
#| label: changsha-mann-kendall

changsha_mk <- cbg %>%
  summarise(
    mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star)))
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest_wider(mk)

knitr::kable(
  changsha_mk,
  digits = 5,
  caption = "Mann-Kendall test for Changsha's Gi* series"
)
```

For Changsha, tau is `r round(changsha_mk$tau, 3)` and the p-value, reported as `sl`, is `r format.pval(changsha_mk$sl, digits = 3)`. The positive tau indicates an upward trend in the local Gi* series. At the 5% level, the result is `r ifelse(changsha_mk$sl < .05, "statistically significant", "not statistically significant")`. Tau describes the direction of ordering; it is not an annual growth rate.

### Testing all counties

The same test is repeated for each county. Sorting by the p-value brings the strongest evidence of monotonic change to the top.

```{r}
#| label: all-county-mann-kendall

county_mk <- gi_stars %>%
  group_by(County) %>%
  summarise(
    mk = list(unclass(Kendall::MannKendall(gi_star))),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  tidyr::unnest_wider(mk)

emerging <- county_mk %>%
  arrange(sl, desc(abs(tau))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10) %>%
  transmute(
    County,
    Tau = tau,
    `p-value` = sl,
    Direction = if_else(tau > 0, "Upward Gi* trend", "Downward Gi* trend")
  )

knitr::kable(
  emerging,
  digits = 6,
  caption = "Ten strongest monotonic Gi* trends"
)
```

The three smallest p-values belong to `r paste(emerging$County[1:3], collapse = ", ")`. This table identifies a change in local spatial association, not yet a complete EHSA class. The final classification also considers which individual years were significant hot spots or cold spots.

## Performing Emerging Hot Spot Analysis

`emerging_hotspot_analysis()` combines the annual Gi* histories with the Mann-Kendall trend. Following the chapter, one time lag and 99 simulations are used. The package’s classification threshold is explicitly set to 0.01, its current default. This final call builds its own row-standardised contiguity weights; it does **not** inherit the inverse-distance weights used above. Its output `p_value` is the Mann–Kendall trend p-value. The internal bin test uses a folded simulation tail; it should not be described as a two-sided 5% test or as FDR-adjusted. The chapter introduces FDR conceptually, but this call does not apply it.

```{r}
#| label: run-ehsa

set.seed(6262026)

ehsa <- emerging_hotspot_analysis(
  x = GDPPC_st,
  .var = "GDPPC",
  k = 1,
  nsim = 99,
  threshold = 0.01,
  include_gi = TRUE
)

ehsa_display <- ehsa %>%
  mutate(
    classification = classification %>%
      str_replace("^oscilating", "oscillating") %>%
      str_to_sentence()
  )
```

### Distribution of EHSA classes

```{r}
#| label: ehsa-class-chart
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of EHSA classes across Hunan counties"
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5

class_counts <- ehsa_display %>%
  count(classification, sort = TRUE)

ggplot(
  class_counts,
  aes(x = reorder(classification, n), y = n)
) +
  geom_col(fill = "#3182bd", width = 0.72) +
  geom_text(aes(label = n), hjust = -0.25, size = 3.8) +
  coord_flip(clip = "off") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.10))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Number of counties") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

The largest class is **`r class_counts$classification[1]`**, with `r class_counts$n[1]` counties. These labels depend on the simulation seed, threshold and package implementation. The count chart includes all counties; the map below applies an additional trend filter.

### Mapping significant EHSA results

The EHSA table is joined to the county polygons by the named county field. In keeping with the chapter, only counties with Mann-Kendall p-values below 0.05 are coloured. The legend is placed outside the map so it does not cover any county.

```{r}
#| label: join-ehsa

hunan_ehsa <- hunan %>%
  left_join(
    ehsa_display,
    by = join_by(County == location)
  )

ehsa_sig <- hunan_ehsa %>%
  filter(p_value < 0.05)

stopifnot(
  nrow(hunan_ehsa) == nrow(hunan),
  nrow(ehsa_sig) == sum(ehsa_display$p_value < 0.05)
)
```

```{r}
#| label: ehsa-map
#| fig-cap: "Significant emerging hot spot and cold spot histories in Hunan"
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7

ehsa_colours <- c(
  "Consecutive hotspot" = "#b2182b",
  "Sporadic hotspot" = "#ef8a62",
  "Oscillating hotspot" = "#fddbc7",
  "Sporadic coldspot" = "#67a9cf",
  "Oscillating coldspot" = "#2166ac",
  "No pattern detected" = "#bdbdbd"
)

# ggplot2 provides the same categorical map without tmap version dependencies.
# Neutral background counties remain visible; only trend-significant classes are coloured.
ggplot(hunan_ehsa) +
  geom_sf(fill = "#f0f2f4", colour = "#9e9e9e", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = ehsa_sig, aes(fill = classification), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ehsa_colours, name = "EHSA class") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Emerging GDPPC hot and cold spot patterns",
       caption = "Only counties with Mann–Kendall p < 0.05 are coloured; grey is not evidence of no clustering.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank())

```

There are `r nrow(ehsa_sig)` counties with a Mann-Kendall p-value below 0.05. The coloured counties pass the trend filter. A county can still have significant hot years yet remain grey if its overall trend is not significant. This distinction matters especially for persistent patterns, which need not have a trend.

### Reading the class labels

The labels summarise both the timing of significant Gi* results and the trend in their intensity.

- **New:** significant only in the final period, with no earlier significant result of the same type.
- **Consecutive:** an uninterrupted run at the end of the series, covering fewer than 90% of all periods.
- **Intensifying or diminishing:** significant in at least 90% of periods, including the last period, with a significant upward or downward intensity trend.
- **Persistent:** significant in at least 90% of periods without a clear upward or downward intensity trend.
- **Sporadic:** significant in some, but fewer than 90%, of the periods and never significant as the opposite type.
- **Oscillating:** significant in the final period but was also significant as the opposite type in an earlier period.
- **Historical:** significant in at least 90% of periods, but not significant in the final period.
- **No pattern detected:** none of the defined histories applies.

The hot spot and cold spot versions use the same timing rules. Their difference is the sign of the underlying local Gi* pattern.

## Assumptions and limitations

- County boundaries and neighbour relationships are treated as constant from 2005 to 2021.
- Inverse-distance weights assume that nearby contiguous counties exert more spatial influence than farther contiguous counties.
- The Mann-Kendall test detects a monotonic direction. It does not require a straight-line trend, but its usual p-value assumes independent observations. Serial dependence can make apparent trends look more convincing than they are.
- GDPPC is analysed as supplied. Without a price adjustment, changes in the raw values may include inflation. The Gi* trend should therefore be read as a change in relative local clustering, not as a pure measure of real economic growth.
- With 99 simulations, the permutation p-values have fairly coarse resolution. More simulations would provide more stable tail probabilities at the cost of longer computation.
- Statistical significance does not explain why a county became a hot spot or cold spot. Policy, industry, population, and measurement changes would need separate investigation.

## Multiple-testing check

Testing 88 counties creates more opportunities for false positives. Benjamini–Hochberg adjustment is added here for the annual-Gi* trend tests. This is a separate check; it does not silently change the chapter’s EHSA labels or correct the internal bin tests.

```{r}
#| label: trend-fdr-check
county_mk <- county_mk |> mutate(q_value = p.adjust(sl, method = "BH"))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  Rule = c("Unadjusted p < 0.05", "BH-adjusted q < 0.05"),
  Counties = c(sum(county_mk$sl < .05), sum(county_mk$q_value < .05))
))
```

## What this exercise shows

The checks establish `r nrow(GDPPC)` observations covering `r nrow(hunan)` counties and `r n_distinct(GDPPC$Year)` years. Changsha’s annual Gi* trend has tau `r round(changsha_mk$tau, 3)` and p = `r format.pval(changsha_mk$sl, digits=3)`. Across all counties, `r sum(county_mk$sl < .05)` annual-Gi* trend tests pass the unadjusted 5% threshold and `r sum(county_mk$q_value < .05)` pass BH adjustment.

An increasing Gi* series means the county’s local spatial context is becoming more concentrated toward high values relative to the reference distribution. It does not establish a causal explanation or measure GDP growth. The final EHSA adds a temporal neighbourhood and classifies the history; that is a different calculation from testing independently computed annual maps.

Run `Rscript setup.R` once, then `quarto render In-class_Ex06.qmd`. The setup file installs the required packages. The labelled chunks execute from imports through the final maps; none depends on a hidden RStudio session.

```{r}
#| label: reproducibility-record
sessionInfo()
```

## References and adaptation notes

- [Kam, Chapter 11: Emerging Hot Spot Analysis](https://r4gdsa.netlify.app/chap11): exercise sequence and Hunan example.
- [sfdep source and documentation](https://github.com/JosiahParry/sfdep): cube construction, local statistics and EHSA implementation.
- [spdep Gi and Gi* documentation](https://r-spatial.github.io/spdep/reference/localG.html): permutation statistics and self-neighbours.
- [Mann–Kendall test, Pacific Northwest National Laboratory](https://vsp.pnnl.gov/help/vsample/design_trend_mann_kendall.htm): interpretation and assumptions.

The interactive chart uses plotly. The categorical map uses ggplot2 rather than tmap; this changes the drawing code, not the EHSA results. The annual permutation count is increased to 999 for a more stable demonstration, while the final EHSA retains the chapter’s 99 simulations so that its computational choices remain visible.
